lines.text: Picture the Epsilon: Pursuing Identity-Level Privacy Guarantees for Images
Arman Zareian Jahromi , Vishnu Bondalakunta , Mohammad Akbar Bin Shah ,
Naimul Haque , Shuangqing
Wei , George T. Amariucai
Kansas State University, Manhattan, KS, USA { zareian, vishnub, mohammadakbar, amariucai } @ksu.edu
Louisiana State University, Baton Rouge,
Abstract —Image-to-image face generators are widely used, and
visual dissimilarity between their outputs and source images
is sometimes treated as evidence of privacy. Auditing whether
these systems satisfy formal identity-level ( ε, δ ) -differential pri-
vacy requires choosing among several distinct routes for con-
verting embedding-space observations into estimates or bounds
on the differential privacy parameter ε . We present a compara-
tive study of four such audits applicable to pre-trained, black-
box face generators: a Gaussian-mechanism reading of per-
identity sensitivity (G AUSS M ECH ); a per-dimension kernel-
density log-ratio aggregated by basic composition (KDE-
LR); an analytical population-level lower bound on pure-
DP ε derived from the maximum mean discrepancy via the
total variation distance (MMD-TV); and a hypothesis-testing
evaluation of a cross-validated classifier’s out-of-fold ROC
(ROC-HT). For each method we make explicit its assumptions,
hyperparameter dependence, finite-sample limitations, and the
regime in which its ε estimate is informative. Applied to Face-
Fusion and InstantID across multiple identity encoders and
reference datasets, the audits consistently reveal substantial
identity distinguishability while reporting markedly different
ε estimates that reflect each method’s distinct assumptions and
finite-sample treatment. In this high-distinguishability regime,
the experiments do not support a reliable ranking of the
four methods. Their relative trade-offs should be evaluated on
partially private mechanisms, which we identify as the natural
next study. The resulting framework places these audits in
a shared identity-level audit setting and clarifies how their
assumptions and finite-sample treatments shape the resulting
differential privacy estimates.
Index Terms —Differential privacy, privacy auditing, face recog-
nition, maximum mean discrepancy, kernel density estimation,
hypothesis testing, image-to-image generation.
1. Introduction
Image-to-image face generators are now part of con-
sumer and prosumer pipelines: face-swap systems such as
FaceFusion [1] replace an identity in a video with an-
other, and diffusion-based zero-shot identity models such
as InstantID [2] synthesize a target person in new poses or
scenes from a few reference images. These systems are not
advertised as privacy-preserving; they are explicitly identity-
transferring or identity-preserving by design. Nevertheless,
LA, USA { naimul.haque, swei } @lsu.edu
visual dissimilarity between an input frame and the gen-
erated output is sometimes treated as informal evidence
of privacy, and as identity-aware image generation gets
used in adjacent pipelines (face anonymization, deepfake
mitigation, privacy-aware data augmentation) the question of
how much identity actually survives the generator becomes
a measurement question. We use FaceFusion and InstantID
as high-distinguishability stress tests. InstantID is designed
to preserve its reference identity; in our FaceFusion setup,
one donor is fixed while the target images vary, allowing
us to test whether the supposedly replaced target identity
remains detectable in the output.
Differential privacy [3], [4] provides a precise ratio con-
straint for such a measurement: a randomized mechanism
M is ( ε, δ ) -DP if its output distributions obey the required
inequality for every adjacent pair of private inputs. Here the
private input is an identity label rather than a database. We
use complete identity adjacency : every two distinct identities
must satisfy the DP inequalities, and each identity indexes
a per-query output distribution. Mathematically, this is a
local-DP condition on the identity-label domain because the
channel acts directly on one private label. We call it dis-
tributional because sampling an image from that identity’s
reference distribution is part of the channel’s randomness.
This secret-indexed view is related to Pufferfish privacy [5].
Several routes exist for turning an embedding-space ob-
servation into an estimate or lower bound on ( ε, δ ) , and the
literature does not converge on a single one. A sensitivity-
and-Gaussian-mechanism reading treats the difference be-
tween per-identity means as the input change and reads
off a closed-form score. This borrows the algebra used
by calibrated feature- and image-space mechanisms [6],
[7], but its retrospective application to arbitrary generated
outputs is a diagnostic rather than a formal lower bound.
A per-dimension kernel-density log-ratio similarly gives a
marginal diagnostic whose coordinate sum is not a joint-
mechanism guarantee. The hypothesis-testing characteriza-
tion of differential privacy [8], [9] translates the popula-
tion operating point of a fixed distinguisher into a lower
bound on ε and underlies empirical DP auditing [10]–
[12]. Prior work also connects maximum mean discrepancy
(MMD) [13] to DP auditing [14]–[16]. We study a pure-
DP chain through total variation [8], [17], [18], compare it
with the tighter Hockey-Stick-based result of Gonza´lez et
al. [16], and evaluate all four routes on a shared task and
data.
This paper presents that comparison for pre-trained,
black-box image-to-image face generators. The four meth-
ods we study are:
G AUSS M ECH (Section 3.1): a Gaussian-mechanism-
inspired diagnostic from the L2 distance between
per-identity means and a pooled residual scale;
KDE-LR (Section 3.2): a basic-composition sum
of per-dimension kernel-density log-ratios, with a
smoothing weight α ;
MMD-TV (Section 3.3): an analytical lower bound
on pure-DP ε derived from the maximum mean
discrepancy through the chain MMD ≤ 2 d TV and
the TV characterization of pure DP;
• ROC-HT (Section 3.4): a hypothesis-testing eval-
uation based on the out-of-fold receiver operating
characteristic of a cross-validated classifier.
For each method we make explicit its assumptions, its
hyperparameter dependence, and the regime in which its
ε estimate or lower bound is informative. We then evaluate
all four on the same audit task across two identity encoders
(ArcFace, FaceNet), two reference datasets (VGGFace2,
CelebA), and two generators (FaceFusion, InstantID), for
a total of eight conditions.
Contributions.
• We present a comparative framework that places
G AUSS M ECH , KDE-LR, MMD-TV, and ROC-
HT side by side on the same identity-substitution
audit task with a shared per-condition pair list and
a common 100-pair summary, and clarifies for each
method which quantities are formal ε lower bounds
and which are finite-sample diagnostics.
• We document the pure-DP MMD-TV specialization
obtained by composing MMD ≤ 2 d TV [17] with
the total variation characterization of pure DP [8],
[18], state its population and finite-sample limits,
and compare it explicitly with the tighter Hockey-
Stick-based MMD result used in prior auditing
• We add a finite-sample ROC-HT protocol that sep-
arates pair and threshold selection from evalua-
tion: all adaptive choices use a development split,
while fixed classifiers and thresholds for 40 selected,
vertex-disjoint identity pairs are evaluated once on
untouched data with simultaneous one-sided exact
confidence bounds.
• We empirically evaluate the four methods on eight
(encoder × dataset × generator) conditions of Face-
Fusion and InstantID auditing. The four audits con-
sistently reveal substantial identity distinguishabil-
ity; the reserved-test protocol certifies positive ε
lower bounds for all 20 selected VGGFace2 pairs,
with 15 exceeding ε = 1 , while its loss of
power on CelebA exposes the sample cost of finite-
sample certification. The methods’ different scales
still do not support a reliable ranking in this high-
distinguishability regime.
The honest finding is that the four methods cannot be
ranked on these generators because the audited regime is
already highly distinguishable: every method reports sub-
stantial identity signal, but the reported numbers are con-
trolled by method-specific assumptions, endpoint behavior,
or looseness rather than by a shared notion of tightness.
None of the evaluated off-the-shelf generators combines
a known identity-level guarantee under our threat model
with tunable, intermediate distinguishability. We therefore
outline in Section 5 a controlled calibrated-noise benchmark
on which the four methods could produce non-endpoint,
comparable ε values.
2. Background and Threat Model

2.3. Face Identity Encoders and Generators
A face identity encoder is a function ϕ : I →
R d
mapping an image x ∈ I to an identity em-
bedding. We use precomputed 512-dimensional Arc-
Face/InsightFace embeddings [19], [20] and precomputed
512-dimensional InceptionResnet-V1 embeddings produced
with facenet-pytorch [21]. The repository does not
preserve the exact encoder checkpoint identifiers, so we do
not infer a training set or checkpoint variant from the arrays
alone. Before every audit, each embedding is L2-normalized
to the unit hypersphere. We treat ϕ as a fixed identity-
oriented representation, not as ground truth; encoder errors
propagate into all four audits (Section 8).
We audit two generators from distinct architectural fam-
ilies. FaceFusion [1] is an open-source face-swap system,
and InstantID [2] is a diffusion-based zero-shot identity
generator. In every FaceFusion condition, a single donor
is held fixed and the images associated with each dataset
identity are supplied as targets; the stored identity label
therefore denotes the target identity. InstantID conditions
group outputs by the reference identity used for gener-
ation. The official InstantID pipeline uses InsightFace’s
antelopev2 identity model; if the precomputed outputs
followed that default, the ArcFace/InsightFace audit partially
overlaps the representation used to condition generation.
The absent generation manifest prevents us from verifying
that configuration, and the FaceNet conditions provide the
cleaner cross-encoder check. We use both systems as high-
distinguishability stress tests rather than privacy mecha-
nisms.

2.5. Threat Model
Distributional mechanism. Let P id be the reference-dataset
distribution of images labeled with identity id , and let R
collect any internal randomness of the generator. For In-
stantID, X ∼ P id is a reference image and the generated
image is Y = g ID ( X ; R ) . For FaceFusion, X ∼ P id is a
target image, one donor image d 0 is fixed for every identity,
and the generated image is Y = g FF ( X ; d 0 , R ) . The pre-
encoder image-output channel and the embedding channel
actually audited are
M
img (id) = Law( Y | X ∼ P id , R ∼ P R ) ,
M ϕ (id) = Law( ϕ ( Y ) | X ∼ P id , R ∼ P R ) .
Thus identity-conditioned image sampling is part of the
channel being measured. Each CelebA identity contributes
26–35 usable generated embeddings, whereas each VG-
GFace2 identity contributes 90–100. Operationally, the
channel models one query whose image is drawn from the
stated identity-conditioned population. It does not guarantee
privacy for an arbitrary fixed photograph selected by a user,
because that deployment conditions on one particular image
rather than averaging over X ∼ P id . This secret-indexed
family resembles the Pufferfish organization of secrets and
data-generating distributions [5], while Definition 1 imposes
the ordinary pairwise DP inequalities. For InstantID, the
private label is the reference identity. For FaceFusion, it
is the target identity; the donor d 0 is identical for both
classes in every pairwise test. The classifier receives one
generated 512-dimensional embedding and predicts which
of two target identities produced it, so target separation
cannot be caused by changing the donor.
Adjacency and post-processing. We use complete adja-
cency over identity labels: any two distinct labels id A and
id B are adjacent. This is the DP convention specifying
which input pairs must satisfy the inequality, not a claim
that the identities are similar. Because M ϕ = ϕ ◦ M img
and the encoder is deterministic, any DP guarantee for the
generated-image distribution M img would also hold after
encoding. Conversely, a confidence-certified violation for
M ϕ refutes the same proposed guarantee for M img . Passing
an encoder audit does not prove privacy of the generated
image.

Adversary. The adversary observes one draw from M ϕ and
tests which identity distribution produced it. The precom-

3. Four Audit Methods
3.1. G AUSS M ECH : Gaussian Calibration Diagnos-
tic
G AUSS M ECH applies the familiar Gaussian-calibration
algebra to the distance between per-identity means and an
empirical residual scale. The textbook sufficient calibra-
tion assumes additive, input-independent isotropic Gaus-
sian noise, global sensitivity, and is commonly stated for
ε ∈ (0 , 1) [4]. Those conditions do not hold here, and invert-
ing the expression to obtain scores in the tens extrapolates
beyond that stated regime. We therefore treat the result only
as a Gaussian signal-to-noise diagnostic.

Using the larger of the two residual scales produces a

Pros.
• Closed form and interpretable. The score reduces
each pair to mean displacement divided by a residual
scale.
• Cheap. Once per-identity means and residual scales
are computed, each pair costs O ( d ) .
Cons.
• Gaussian residual assumption fails empirically. Af-
ter L2 normalization, the per-dimension residual dis-
tributions are concentrated but non-Gaussian (Fig-
ure 1). A Shapiro–Wilk test of Gaussianity [22]
on the pooled within-identity residuals rejects at
p < 10 on 509 of 512 dimensions for the canon-
ical ArcFace+VGGFace2+InstantID condition, and
on a majority of the 512 dimensions in all eight of
the conditions we audit.
• Isotropic noise assumption collapses cross-
dimensional variation. The single σ averages the
per-dimension residual variance into one number,
discarding heteroscedasticity across dimensions.
• Finite-sample treatment is implicit. Empirical means
and variances are substituted without a confidence
correction.
• Single per-pair number. The per-pair ε does not
separate mechanism noise from sampling noise; an
identity with high within-identity variance receives
a small ε , which can mask identity leakage in a
different geometric direction.
Hyperparameters. We fix δ = 10 for this diagnostic
and use the root-mean-square within-identity residual per
coordinate, σ id , as the scale. Because the method is not a
valid Gaussian-mechanism inversion for these generators, its
δ should not be compared directly with the pure-DP MMD-
TV and ROC-HT formulas.

has a data-driven default; the third trades off audit cost for
tightness of the per-pair maximum.
3.4. ROC-HT: Hypothesis-Testing Bound from a
Classifier’s ROC
ROC-HT applies the hypothesis-testing characterization
of differential privacy [8], [9] to a classifier trained to dis-

Pros.
• Distribution-free at the population level. Equation 15
follows the Kairouz–Oh–Viswanath characterization
of pure DP at δ = 0 . For a fixed population dis-
tinguisher, it requires no parametric model for the
output distribution.
• Improves with the distinguisher. A stronger fixed
population test can yield a larger lower bound.
• Cross-validation reduces training-set optimism. Out-
of-fold operating points are not evaluated on the
same examples used to train each fold’s classifier.
This reduces training-set optimism, but it is not a
substitute for a finite-sample confidence certificate.
Cons.
• Diverges at ROC endpoints. The raw empirical OOF
value is + ∞ whenever the ROC contains an oper-
ating point with TPR = 1 and FPR < 1 , or with
FPR = 0 and TPR > 0 . This endpoint divergence
is algebraically correct for Equation 15, but it does
not by itself imply exact zero-error separation. We
therefore report AUC and separately track the stricter
exact corner ( FPR , TPR) = (0 , 1) .
• Sensitive to classifier choice. The bound is only
as tight as the trained classifier. A random forest
in place of logistic regression returns a different
operating point on the same data, which is why we
report classifier sensitivity as a diagnostic rather than
treating one classifier as canonical.
• The out-of-fold value is not a certificate. Five fold-
specific classifiers produce the pooled scores, and the
maximizing threshold is selected on those same out-
of-fold predictions. We therefore keep this quantity
as a diagnostic and use a separate reserved-test pro-
tocol with exact simultaneous confidence treatment
in Section 4.3.
• Sample-size dependence in the endpoint regime.
The OOF value + ∞ is an empirical finite-sample
statement about the observed ROC. A larger audit
could reveal overlap and move the relevant operating
points away from the zero-denominator endpoints.
Hyperparameters. ROC-HT has three: (i) the classifier
family (we use logistic regression and include a random-
forest sensitivity check in Section 4.4); (ii) the number of
cross-validation folds (we use 5); (iii) the per-pair sample
size, which is fixed by the data ( n ≈ 100 on VGGFace2,
n ≈ 30 on CelebA). The first is the principal lever for tight-
ening the bound; the second has the conventional choice; the
third is determined by the reference dataset.
4. Comparative Experimental Evaluation

Datasets. We use selected identity subsets from VG-

The out-of-fold ROC summaries above are broad diag-

4.5. Honest Comparison
The methods cannot be ranked from these experiments.
The classifier and MMD tests provide direct empirical evi-
dence of identity distinguishability, the reserved-test ROC
protocol certifies all 20 selected VGGFace2 pairs under
one simultaneous confidence family, and the two modeling
diagnostics are consistent with the same qualitative con-
clusion. Their numerical scales differ for method-specific
reasons and do not reveal relative tightness at intermediate
privacy levels. A controlled benchmark with a known pri-
vacy guarantee and non-endpoint behavior is needed for that
comparison.

5. Discussion
5.1. Why the Four Methods Cannot Be Ranked
Here
Not every number in Table 1 has the same formal
status. MMD-TV is a population pure-DP lower-bound
route evaluated here with an uncertified sample estimate;
ROC-HT is a hypothesis-testing route whose broad OOF
estimate diverges at ROC endpoints, while Table 2 gives
separately certified selected-pair bounds; G AUSS M ECH and
KDE-LR are diagnostics tied to modeling and aggregation
assumptions. A natural question is still which audit is most
informative. On the eight conditions of Table 1, that ques-
tion is not well-posed. The generators are already highly
distinguishable, and the reported values are dominated by
each method’s assumptions, confidence treatment, or end-
point behavior: KDE-LR reports values in the thousands,
G AUSS M ECH in the tens, MMD-TV below one, and ROC-
HT has high AUC with raw endpoint-divergent OOF values.
The four methods therefore do not separate cleanly on these
generators.
5.2. A Benchmark on Which the Four Methods
Could Differ
The cleanest comparison would use a per-query bench-
mark with a known privacy guarantee and a controllable
range of distinguishability. One construction is to add cal-
ibrated isotropic Gaussian noise to the normalized encoder
output:
M ν (id) = ϕ ( g ( X )) + ξ,
X ∼ P id ,
ξ ∼ N (0 , ν I d ) .
where P id is the identity’s source-image distribution and
ν is varied. Because L2 normalization places every output
on the unit sphere S , the L2 distance between any two
outputs is at most 2 (the diameter of S ). The per-pair L2
sensitivity of the mean-shift mechanism this benchmark is
calibrated against therefore satisfies ∆ 2 ≤ 2 , so the analytic
Gaussian-mechanism calibration of Balle and Wang [30] at
a fixed nonzero δ supplies a reference upper guarantee. The
audits could then be compared against that reference as ν
increases and the ROC leaves its endpoint regime. This ex-
periment would evaluate calibration and sensitivity, not turn
the original black-box generators into certified mechanisms.
Such a controlled benchmark is needed because none of
the evaluated off-the-shelf generators provides both a known
guarantee for our identity channel and tunable intermediate
distinguishability.
5.3. Which Method to Use When
The four methods are not interchangeable. G AUSS M ECH
is a cheap diagnostic for mechanisms plausibly dominated
by additive Gaussian noise. KDE-LR exposes coordinate-
level marginal differences but its sum is not a joint DP
guarantee. MMD-TV supplies a classifier-free population
lower-bound route, provided its sample estimate receives
a one-sided finite-sample treatment. ROC-HT can exploit
a strong distinguisher; our reserved-test protocol shows
how a fixed, independently evaluated test and simultaneous
confidence correction turn that route into a finite-sample
certificate, at the cost of reduced power on small test sets.
These requirements, rather than the magnitudes in Table 1,
should determine the audit choice.
6. Related Work
DP auditing. Jagielski, Ullman, and Oprea [10] audit DP-
SGD using membership-inference attacks; Nasr et al. [11]
instantiate strong canary adversaries; and Steinke, Nasr, and
Jagielski [12] develop single-run auditing. These works use
hypothesis tests to lower-bound effective privacy parame-
ters. Their neighborhoods and mechanisms differ from ours:
they audit training algorithms under record-level changes,
whereas we study an inference-time distribution indexed by
identity labels. The hypothesis-testing conversion is not our
contribution; our focus is its comparison with three other
embedding-space routes in this identity-level setting.
Training-data privacy in generative models. Carlini et
al. [31] demonstrate extraction of memorized diffusion-
model training examples, while Hu and Pang [32] study
membership inference against denoising diffusion models.
Those works ask whether training records are memorized or
identifiable. We instead ask whether a generated-output dis-
tribution is distinguishable across two input identity labels.
The threat models are complementary and neither result
implies the other.
DP for image and generative mechanisms. DP-SGD pro-
tects a training algorithm under a specified dataset neigh-
borhood [33], whereas feature-space and local-DP image
mechanisms add calibrated noise to an image or represen-
tation before subsequent processing [6], [7]. These guar-
antees answer different questions from our distributional
inference-time audit. Our G AUSS M ECH diagnostic borrows
the algebra of Gaussian calibration, but neither it nor KDE-
LR inherits a guarantee from those prior mechanisms when
applied retrospectively to arbitrary black-box outputs.
MMD, total variation, and the hypothesis-testing charac-
terization of DP. The kernel two-sample formulation used
here follows Gretton et al. [13]. Sriperumbudur et al. [17]
studied its relationship to other integral probability metrics,
including the comparison underlying Lemma 1. The TV and
hypothesis-testing characterizations of DP follow Kairouz,
Oh, and Viswanath [8], Ghazi and Issa [18], and the f -
DP formulation of Dong, Roth, and Su [9]. Kernel-based
DP auditors include Domingo-Enrich and Mroueh [14], DP-
Auditorium [15], and the sequential MMD audit of Gonza´lez
et al. [16]. The mathematical pieces of MMD-TV are
therefore pre-existing; our contribution is their explicit pure-
DP specialization and their assumption-matched empirical
comparison beside three other identity-level audit routes.
7. Ethics and Dual Use
This work measures identity leakage in face-generation
systems and therefore involves sensitive biometric data and
dual-use risk. Its intended use is defensive evaluation of
privacy claims. The same methods could support identity
recognition, so we report aggregate embedding-level results
and do not release generated faces or identity-specific attack
artifacts. The study uses selected subsets of public face
datasets and precomputed outputs; it collects no new par-
ticipant data, conducts no user study, and does not attempt
to re-identify unnamed individuals. Public availability does
not remove concerns about consent, demographic bias, or
downstream misuse. Encoder performance may vary across
demographic groups, but the available metadata do not
support a subgroup analysis; this limits the fairness con-
clusions that can be drawn. Artifact releases should exclude
face images, minimize identity-linked metadata, document
dataset licenses and model terms, and state the intended
defensive use.
8. Limitations and Future Work
Generators, data, and provenance. The comparison is
limited to precomputed FaceFusion and InstantID out-
puts built from selected VGGFace2 and CelebA iden-
tities. The loader removes missing and zero-norm vec-
tors; after filtering, the ArcFace+CelebA+FaceFusion and
FaceNet+CelebA+FaceFusion conditions each retain one du-
plicated vector. The FaceFusion protocol fixes one donor and
varies target images by dataset identity, so the stored labels
represent target identities. However, the repository lacks a
versioned generation manifest containing exact revisions,
prompts, seeds, checkpoints, and the donor asset identifier.
We therefore cannot reproduce image generation from this
repository alone or attribute differences to a specific gen-
erator revision. Other generators, data distributions, donors,
or preprocessing choices may produce different results.
Encoder as the identity oracle. The four audits treat
the identity encoder ϕ as a fixed proxy for identity. A
generator that leaks identity as either encoder defines it
but not as a human defines it would still register strong
distinguishability under our audits. We probe encoder de-
pendence with ArcFace/InsightFace and FaceNet representa-
tions (Section 2.3); the qualitative verdict is preserved across
both, although the numerical values shift. Exact checkpoint
identifiers for the precomputed embeddings are unavailable.
In addition, InstantID’s official pipeline uses the ArcFace-
family antelopev2 representation for conditioning, so
the ArcFace+InstantID result may benefit from representa-
tion overlap; FaceNet+InstantID is the cleaner cross-encoder
check.
High-distinguishability regime. The principal limitation of
this paper is that the audited generators are already highly
distinguishable (Section 4.5). The comparison is honest
about this: it does not allow us to claim that one method is
tighter than another at intermediate privacy levels. The natu-
ral follow-up is the calibrated-noise mechanism sketched in
Section 5, on which the four methods would produce non-
endpoint, comparable ε values across a sweep of the noise
scale.
Per-query versus multi-query privacy. Definition 1 is a
per-query identity-level notion: the mechanism output is
one generated embedding, and the N images per identity
are used to estimate the corresponding per-identity output
distribution. We do not claim a group-privacy guarantee
for releasing the full generated batch from an identity. An
adversary who observes many independent outputs from
the same identity can compose evidence across queries,
and translating the per-query audit numbers to a multi-
query release requires specifying the composition model
and the number of queries. We therefore avoid dividing
or multiplying the reported ε values by N in the main
comparison.
Finite-sample certification. The population MMD and
hypothesis-testing inequalities are valid, but the reported
MMD-TV and broad OOF ROC sample estimates are not
confidence-certified lower bounds. Section 4.3 adds a sep-
arate reserved-test ROC evaluation with simultaneous exact
confidence treatment for five development-selected, vertex-
disjoint pairs per condition. Its guarantees are conditional
on iid sampling from the defined P id , concern adaptively
selected stress-test pairs rather than a representative pair
sample, and lose all power on the smaller CelebA test
sets under the global 40-pair correction. A one-sided MMD
concentration or sequential treatment remains future work.
Neighborhood and deployment choices. Definition 1 treats
identity-conditioned image sampling from P id as mechanism
randomness. It does not establish DP for a fixed user-
selected photograph or for releasing multiple outputs. In the
FaceFusion audit the donor is fixed, so the reported values
do not characterize privacy under a changing-donor neigh-
borhood. Per-image, prompt, variable-donor, and dataset-
level neighborhoods require new mechanism definitions and,
in some cases, different sampling and sensitivity analyses;
the current numerical results do not transfer automatically.
Representation dependence. Every conclusion is condi-
tional on the selected encoders and preprocessing. Using
two encoders is a robustness check, not proof that all identity
information in the pixels is captured. Extension to another
modality would require a new threat model, representation
validation, and finite-sample study rather than a direct reuse
of the reported numbers.
9. Conclusion
We presented a comparative study of four empirical
differential privacy audits applicable to pre-trained, black-
box image-to-image face generators: G AUSS M ECH , KDE-
LR, MMD-TV, and ROC-HT. For each audit we made
explicit its definition, assumptions, hyperparameter depen-
dence, finite-sample status, and route from an embedding-
space measurement to an ε diagnostic or population lower
bound. We documented the MMD-TV pure-DP special-
ization for positive-definite kernels satisfying k ( x, x ) ≤ 1 ,
aligned the empirical comparison on common identity pairs,
and added a development-selected, reserved-test ROC-HT
certificate with simultaneous exact confidence control.
Across the eight encoder × dataset × generator con-
ditions, the classifier and two-sample tests reveal substan-
tial identity-distinguishing signal. Our finite-sample ROC
protocol (Section 4.3) sets aside an untouched test split
per identity: pair selection, classifier fitting, and threshold
selection use only the development split, and the test split is
reserved for one fixed evaluation. Evaluated on this reserved
test split, the protocol certifies positive selected-pair ε lower
bounds for all 20 VGGFace2 stress-test pairs under one
simultaneous 95% confidence family; 15 exceed ε = 1 .
Its inability to certify the much smaller CelebA test sets
despite high AUC makes the sample cost of finite-sample DP
auditing explicit. The modeling diagnostics are consistent
with the distinguishability conclusion, but their numerical
values differ because of assumptions, aggregation, finite-
sample treatment, and ROC endpoint behavior, not because
the experiments identify a tightest audit. G AUSS M ECH and
KDE-LR are not formal joint-mechanism lower bounds
here; the MMD-TV and broad out-of-fold ROC-HT values
remain uncertified sample estimates, even though the ROC-
HT values produced by the separate reserved-test protocol
of Section 4.3 are certified. A benchmark with a known
privacy guarantee whose audited ROC keeps every operating
point strictly inside the unit square, so that no point has
FPR = 0 or TPR = 1 and the hypothesis-testing plug-in
of Equation 15 returns finite values rather than the endpoint
divergences observed here, is therefore the necessary next
step for comparing calibration and tightness.
